concepts_used: Article 22: Dual Structure — Ordinary Arrest vs. Preventive Detention

solution.concept_anchor: Article 22 dual structure — punitive vs preventive
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students often assume that since both relate to personal liberty, Article 22 applies uniformly to all forms of detention.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Article 22 does not apply uniformly — it has two distinct parts for two distinct legal situations.
Eliminate (b): Preventive detention involves no trial and precedes any offence, so it cannot be described as post-conviction detention.
Eliminate (d): Article 21 and Article 22 must be read together post-Maneka Gandhi — they do not operate in total isolation.
Confirm (c): Articles 22(1)&(2) govern ordinary/punitive arrest while Articles 22(3)–(7) constitute a separate code for preventive detention — this is the correct structural description.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students who have a surface-level understanding assume that Article 22 provides a single uniform set of protections for all detained persons. The trap lies in the fact that Article 22 is internally bifurcated — the first two clauses are about ordinary criminal arrest and the remaining clauses (3–7) constitute a separate legal universe governing preventive detention. A person arrested under a preventive detention law cannot invoke Article 22(1) or 22(2), and this structural distinction is the single most exploited trap in this area.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 22 of the Constitution is uniquely structured as two parallel codes within a single Article. Clauses (1) and (2) protect persons arrested in the ordinary course of law — someone arrested on suspicion of a crime. Clauses (3) through (7) exclusively govern preventive detention, where a person is detained not for a past offence but to prevent a future one.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Article 22 does not apply uniformly to all detentions. Its two parts address entirely different legal situations with different protections.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Preventive detention precedes any offence or trial; characterising it as post-conviction misrepresents its constitutional basis.
• Option (c) — Correct: This accurately captures the dual-code structure of Article 22 — punitive arrest (22(1)&(2)) and preventive detention (22(3)–(7)) operate in separate legal universes.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Post-Maneka Gandhi (1978), Articles 21 and 22 must be read together; they do not operate in total isolation.

Value Addition:
• Preventive detention is constitutionally recognised — it is one of the few democracies where preventive detention has an explicit constitutional footing.
• Article 22 safeguards are minimum guarantees — Parliament/State can legislate additional protections.
• The silo theory from A.K. Gopalan (1950) treating each Article independently was overruled by Maneka Gandhi (1978).

concepts_used: Rights of Arrested Persons Under Article 22(1) and 22(2)

solution.concept_anchor: Article 22(1)(2) rights of arrested persons — 24-hour rule

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 22(1), an arrested person must be informed of the grounds of arrest and has the right to consult a legal practitioner of their own choosing.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 22(1) explicitly guarantees both the right to be informed of grounds of arrest and the right to consult and be defended by a lawyer of one's choice — these are two of the three mandatory rights.

statement_analysis.statement: The requirement to produce an arrested person before a magistrate within 24 hours includes the time spent in transit from the place of arrest to the magistrate's court.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 22(2) and its constitutional interpretation specifically exclude travel time from place of arrest to the magistrate from the 24-hour computation — the period runs from arrest, but transit time is deducted.

statement_analysis.statement: Beyond the 24-hour period, further detention of an arrested person is permissible only under the authority of a magistrate, not the police.
statement_analysis.reason: After the mandatory production before a magistrate within 24 hours, any further detention must be authorised by the magistrate — the police have no independent authority to continue detention beyond this point.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is deceptive because students who correctly identify Statement 2 as false often doubt Statement 3, assuming it overstates judicial authority over post-arrest detention.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Article 22(1) guarantees both grounds-of-arrest communication and right to consult a lawyer — Statement 1 is correct.
Verify Statement 2: The 24-hour rule explicitly EXCLUDES transit time — the statement says 'includes', making it incorrect.
Verify Statement 3: Post-24-hours, only magistrate authority permits continued detention — Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct; Statement 2 is incorrect — select option (b): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the primary trap. The 24-hour rule appears simple, but many students assume it runs from arrest to production as a continuous block including travel. The Constitution specifically excludes travel time, meaning a person arrested in a remote location gets the full 24 hours of substantive time before the magistrate — the journey does not eat into this entitlement. This distinction is frequently tested because it appears in the text of Article 22 itself, yet students overlook it.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 22(1) and (2) constitute the Constitution's core protection against arbitrary ordinary arrest. Three mandatory safeguards flow from these clauses: (i) right to be informed of grounds of arrest, (ii) right to consult a lawyer of one's choice, and (iii) right to be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 22(1) explicitly confers both grounds-communication and lawyer-consultation rights — this is textually unambiguous.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The 24-hour computation excludes travel time from the place of arrest to the court. Saying it 'includes' transit time inverts the constitutional provision and would defeat its protective purpose.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Once the 24-hour window expires, the police have no independent authority — only a magistrate can authorise continued detention under Section 167 CrPC (now BNSS).

Value Addition:
• D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997) expanded these safeguards further, making additional procedural requirements (such as informing relatives) enforceable under Article 21.
• The lawyer's right under Article 22(1) is to a lawyer 'of one's choice' — the state is not obliged to provide one at this stage (free legal aid flows separately from Article 39A).
• Violation of Article 22(1) or (2) does not automatically invalidate prosecution — but it makes continued detention unlawful.

concepts_used: Exceptions to Article 22(1) and 22(2) Protections — Article 22(3)

solution.concept_anchor: Article 22(3) — enemy aliens excluded from both protection sets

statement_analysis.statement: Enemy aliens are denied the protections available under Article 22(1) and (2) but retain the safeguards applicable to preventive detenues under Article 22(3)–(7).
statement_analysis.reason: Article 22(3) excludes enemy aliens from BOTH sets of protections — neither the ordinary arrest rights nor the preventive detention safeguards apply to them as a matter of constitutional right.

statement_analysis.statement: A citizen of a friendly foreign nation arrested in India on suspicion of a criminal offence cannot invoke the protections under Article 22(1) and (2).
statement_analysis.reason: Article 22(3) excludes only 'enemy aliens' — a foreign national who is not an enemy alien retains Article 22(1) and (2) protections. Friendly foreign nationals are not excluded.

statement_analysis.statement: Persons arrested under any law providing for preventive detention are explicitly excluded from the protections available under Article 22(1) and (2).
statement_analysis.reason: Article 22(3)(b) expressly removes the Article 22(1) and (2) protections from persons arrested under preventive detention laws — they fall under the separate regime of Article 22(4)–(7).

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students who correctly identify Statement 1 as wrong may assume Statement 2 is also wrong without recognising that Statement 3 is actually correct, leading them to select 'only one is incorrect' rather than 'only two are incorrect.'
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Enemy aliens lose BOTH sets of protections under Article 22 — the statement saying they retain preventive detention safeguards is wrong.
Evaluate Statement 2: Only enemy aliens are excluded; a friendly foreign national retains Article 22(1)&(2) protections — this statement is also wrong.
Evaluate Statement 3: Article 22(3)(b) explicitly excludes preventive detenues from 22(1)&(2) — this is textually correct and therefore NOT the incorrect statement.
Statements 1 and 2 are incorrect; select option (c): 1 and 2.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits the most dangerous misconception — that enemy aliens, while losing ordinary arrest protections, still benefit from the preventive detention safeguards in Article 22(4)–(7). The Constitution creates a total exclusion for enemy aliens: they are outside both protective frameworks. Statement 2 targets students who conflate 'foreign national' with 'enemy alien' — only nationals of countries at war with India qualify as enemy aliens; all other foreign nationals retain Article 22(1)&(2) rights.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 22(3) carves out two categories of persons who are denied the protections of Article 22(1) and (2): (a) enemy aliens and (b) persons arrested under any preventive detention law.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Enemy aliens are constitutionally excluded from BOTH sets of Article 22 protections. The Constitution does not give them the alternative safeguards of 22(4)–(7) — they exist in a rights-free zone under Article 22.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: A foreign national from a friendly country is not an 'enemy alien.' Only nationals of countries at war with India qualify. Friendly foreign nationals arrested on ordinary criminal charges retain full Article 22(1) and (2) protections.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Article 22(3)(b) expressly excludes preventive detenues from 22(1)&(2) rights — this is the correct and uncontroversial exclusion.

Value Addition:
• The term 'enemy alien' is not defined in the Constitution itself — its meaning is drawn from international law and the Enemy Aliens Act.
• The constitutional exclusion of enemy aliens from all Article 22 protections is considered a significant derogation and has attracted academic criticism.
• A friendly foreign national has the same Article 22 rights as a citizen during ordinary arrest.

Parliament's Power to Prescribe Detention Beyond 3 Months — Article 22(7): The Legislative Override

solution.concept_anchor: Article 22(4) three-month ceiling and 44th Amendment non-enforcement

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 22(4), no person can be detained under a preventive detention law for more than 3 months without an Advisory Board reporting sufficient cause for continued detention.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 22(4) sets the default ceiling at 3 months — detention beyond this period requires the Advisory Board to report sufficient cause before the 3-month period expires.

statement_analysis.statement: The 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978) reduced the maximum permissible detention period without Advisory Board reference from 3 months to 2 months, and this amendment is currently in force.
statement_analysis.reason: While the 44th Amendment did seek to reduce the period to 2 months, its relevant provisions were never brought into force — the original 3-month rule continues to operate.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 22(7) empowers both Parliament and State Legislatures to prescribe, by law, circumstances permitting detention beyond 3 months without Advisory Board reference.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 22(7) grants this power exclusively to Parliament (the Union Legislature) — State Legislatures cannot invoke this provision to authorise detention beyond 3 months without Advisory Board reference.

statement_analysis.statement: Parliament may, under Article 22(7), both prescribe the circumstances for detention beyond 3 months and fix the maximum permissible period of detention.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 22(7) explicitly empowers Parliament to legislate on both: (a) the circumstances permitting extended detention without Advisory Board, and (b) the maximum period of such detention.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Only three' is a strong distractor because students who correctly identify Statement 2 as false but miss that Statement 3 is also false (conflating Parliament with State Legislatures) will count three correct statements.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: The 3-month default ceiling is constitutionally explicit in Article 22(4) — Correct.
Statement 2: The 44th Amendment's 2-month provision was never notified into force — the claim that it is 'currently in force' makes this Incorrect.
Statement 3: Article 22(7) is an exclusively Parliamentary power — State Legislatures are excluded. Incorrect.
Statement 4: Article 22(7) covers both circumstances and maximum period — Correct. Only two statements are correct; select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Two distinct traps operate here. First, the 44th Amendment trap: the amendment was passed in 1978 but its clause reducing detention to 2 months was deliberately left unimplemented — students who know of the amendment but not its non-enforcement will mark Statement 2 as correct. Second, the federal trap in Statement 3: Article 22(7) is an exclusive Parliamentary power, but students familiar with the Concurrent List (Entry 3) for preventive detention assume State Legislatures share this override power as well.
solution.final_explanation:
Articles 22(4) and 22(7) together define the temporal limits of preventive detention and the legislative override mechanism.

| Statement | Verdict |
|---|---|
| S1: 3-month default ceiling without Advisory Board | Correct |
| S2: 44th Amendment (2-month period) currently in force | Incorrect |
| S3: Both Parliament and States can invoke Article 22(7) | Incorrect |
| S4: Parliament can fix both circumstances and maximum period under 22(7) | Correct |

Only Statements 1 and 4 are correct — 'Only two.'

Value Addition:
• The 44th Amendment (1978) was passed to undo excesses of the Emergency period but several of its provisions were strategically left unimplemented.
• No Parliament has yet enacted legislation invoking the full scope of Article 22(7) — it remains a constitutionally dormant but exam-active provision.
• State Legislatures CAN make preventive detention laws (Entry 3, Concurrent List) but CANNOT invoke Article 22(7)'s override — a critical federal distinction.

Legislative Competence Over Preventive Detention: Union vs. State

solution.concept_anchor: Advisory Board composition and preventive detention legislative competence
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) pairs the Advisory Board with 'a court of record' which sounds judicially plausible but is constitutionally inaccurate — the Board is quasi-judicial, not a court.
elimination_logic: Match A: The Advisory Board must consist of persons who are, or have been, or are qualified to be High Court judges — matches with 3.
Match B: The Advisory Board gives an opinion — it is advisory, not binding; the government is not legally bound to accept it — matches with 1.
Match C: Entry 9 of the Union List covers preventive detention for Defence, Foreign Affairs, Security of India — matches with 4.
Match D: Entry 3 of the Concurrent List covers preventive detention for State security, public order, essential services — matches with 2. Correct combination: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 → option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The most common trap is confusing the Union List entry number (Entry 9) with the Concurrent List entry number (Entry 3) for preventive detention. Students who have memorised one tend to swap the other. Additionally, the characterisation of the Advisory Board as 'not a court' but 'quasi-judicial' is a nuanced distinction — many students assume a body composed of judges must itself be a court, leading them to select an option that incorrectly characterises the Board.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests two distinct areas: the composition and character of the Advisory Board and the constitutional allocation of legislative competence over preventive detention.

The Advisory Board must be composed of persons who are, or have been, or are qualified to be appointed as High Court judges — ensuring a quasi-judicial character. However, it is NOT a court; its report is advisory. The government is not strictly bound, though deviation requires strong justification.

For legislative competence: Entry 9 of the Union List covers preventive detention related to Defence, Foreign Affairs, and Security of India (exclusive Parliamentary domain). Entry 3 of the Concurrent List covers preventive detention for reasons connected with State security, public order, and maintenance of essential services — both Parliament and State Legislatures can legislate here.

Correct matching: A–3, B–1, C–4, D–2.

Value Addition:
• Courts can examine whether the Advisory Board was properly constituted and followed procedure — but cannot substitute their opinion on the sufficiency of cause.
• Goonda Acts passed by States operate under Entry 3 of the Concurrent List.
• The Advisory Board must submit its report within 7 weeks of detention under NSA rules — a procedural timeline tested in MCQs.

upsc_trap_explanation: Students frequently swap Entry 9 (Union List) with Entry 3 (Concurrent List) for preventive detention, particularly because both deal with security-related detention. The Advisory Board characterisation trap (quasi-judicial but not a court) exploits the assumption that a body composed of judges must be a court — a logically seductive but constitutionally incorrect inference.

Preventive Detention and Article 21: The Intersection Post-Maneka Gandhi

solution.concept_anchor: Gopalan to Maneka Gandhi — doctrinal evolution on preventive detention
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because students who recall that Maneka Gandhi came after Gopalan may mix up the intermediate case (Bank Nationalisation, 1970) with the Preventive Detention Act timeline.
elimination_logic: Establish anchor: A.K. Gopalan (1950) is the earliest — it upheld the Preventive Detention Act 1950 and articulated the silo theory.
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) overruled Gopalan's isolation principle — this must come after 1950.
ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla (1976) occurred during the Emergency — this falls between Gopalan (1950) and Maneka Gandhi (1978).
K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) overruled ADM Jabalpur — this is the most recent. Correct order: Gopalan (1950) → ADM Jabalpur (1976) → Maneka Gandhi (1978) → Puttaswamy (2017) → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The classic trap here is confusing the chronological order of ADM Jabalpur (1976) and Maneka Gandhi (1978). Both are Emergency-era and post-Emergency landmark cases respectively, and students often reverse them. Maneka Gandhi came after ADM Jabalpur — it was partly a judicial course-correction after the Emergency era overreach reflected in ADM Jabalpur.
solution.final_explanation:
These four cases mark the doctrinal evolution of the right to life and personal liberty in the context of preventive detention.

Correct sequence: A.K. Gopalan (1950) → ADM Jabalpur (1976) → Maneka Gandhi (1978) → K.S. Puttaswamy (2017).

• Gopalan (1950): Upheld the Preventive Detention Act 1950; established the 'silo theory' — each Article operates independently.
• ADM Jabalpur (1976): During the Emergency, held that Article 21 was the sole repository of the right to life — its suspension meant no challenge to detention; a low point for civil liberties.
• Maneka Gandhi (1978): Overruled Gopalan's isolation; held that Articles 14, 19, and 21 must be read together; procedure must be fair, just, and reasonable.
• Puttaswamy (2017): Overruled ADM Jabalpur; held Articles 20 and 21 are always enforceable — even during Emergency.

Value Addition:
• ADM Jabalpur is considered the darkest chapter in the Supreme Court's history — Justice Khanna's lone dissent in that case is celebrated as a landmark.
• Maneka Gandhi's triple test (Articles 14 + 19 + 21 read together) is now foundational to all fundamental rights adjudication.
• Puttaswamy also recognised the right to privacy as a fundamental right under Article 21.

solution.concept_anchor: No bail in preventive detention — habeas corpus as exclusive remedy
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because students familiar with bail provisions under CrPC/BNSS assume the same mechanism applies here — courts can 'grant bail' pending challenge.
elimination_logic: Identify the legal regime: Keshav is detained under a preventive detention law — this immediately places the case outside the ordinary criminal bail framework.
Eliminate (b): Courts cannot grant bail on merits in preventive detention — bail is a remedy for punitive arrest, not preventive detention.
Eliminate (c): Police authority ends when a detention order is passed under preventive detention law — the detaining authority is the government, not the police.
Eliminate (d): A magistrate has no inherent jurisdiction to extend or modify a preventive detention order — the Advisory Board mechanism governs review.

Confirm (a): The appropriate remedy is a habeas corpus petition under Article 32 (before Supreme Court) or Article 226 (before High Court) — the only judicial route to release in preventive detention.
solution.final_explanation:
Preventive detention and punitive arrest occupy entirely different constitutional universes when it comes to judicial remedies. In ordinary criminal arrests, bail is a statutory entitlement (under CrPC/BNSS) or a constitutional one. In preventive detention, there is no right to bail — the very purpose is to detain without trial.

Keshav's situation calls for a habeas corpus petition under Article 32 (Supreme Court) or Article 226 (High Court). If the court finds the detention order procedurally or substantively invalid — e.g., grounds not communicated in a language he understands — it will order immediate release. This is functionally similar to bail but legally distinct.

• Option (a) — Correct: Habeas corpus is the exclusive judicial remedy; courts examine procedural compliance and validity of the detention order.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Bail on merits does not apply in preventive detention — the bail mechanism presupposes a criminal case pending trial.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Once a detention order is passed, police authority is superseded by the detaining authority (government) — police cannot be directed to release.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Magistrates have no jurisdiction over preventive detention orders; extension and review is through the Advisory Board mechanism.

Value Addition:
• Even one procedural violation (e.g., grounds in an unknown language) renders detention void, not merely voidable.
• Successful habeas corpus results in immediate release — not just a review.
• The detaining authority itself can revoke a detention order at any time.

solution.concept_anchor: Central vs State preventive detention statutes — classification
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) (COFEPOSA) is deceptive because it is less familiar to students and sounds like it might be a state-level law dealing with economic offences.
elimination_logic: Identify the shared attribute: NSA 1980, COFEPOSA 1974, and UAPA are all central (Parliamentary) legislation on preventive detention or security.
Examine MISA: The Maintenance of Internal Security Act was a central law too, but it was repealed in 1977 — however, the question tests classification, not repeal status.
Re-examine: All four are central laws. The question asks which does NOT belong to the same category. Reframe: which is a State-level law?

Goonda Acts are State legislations — none of the options here are Goonda Acts. MISA was the central law passed during the Emergency with the broadest preventive detention scope. The odd one out among 'laws whose primary purpose is preventive detention' is UAPA, which is primarily an anti-terrorism law (punitive + preventive both) — but COFEPOSA is the one law dealing with economic security, not internal security or public order, making it structurally distinct from the others.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: COFEPOSA (Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act, 1974) is a Central preventive detention law but its justification is economic security — conservation of foreign exchange — rather than the conventional categories of national security, public order, or essential services. Students familiar only with security-based detention laws tend to overlook COFEPOSA's classification as a preventive detention statute, making it the structurally distinct entry in this list.
solution.final_explanation:
All four — NSA 1980, COFEPOSA 1974, MISA (repealed), and UAPA — are central (Parliamentary) statutes. However, within this group, three laws (NSA, MISA, UAPA) are primarily premised on security of the State, public order, or national security grounds. COFEPOSA stands apart: it authorises preventive detention on economic security grounds — specifically, preventing smuggling activities and conserving foreign exchange.

• Option (a) NSA 1980: Classic security-based preventive detention — detention for security of India, public order, or essential services.
• Option (b) COFEPOSA 1974: Preventive detention for economic security — conservation of foreign exchange and prevention of smuggling. This is the structurally distinct entry.
• Option (c) MISA (repealed 1977): Security-based preventive detention used during the Emergency.
• Option (d) UAPA: Anti-terrorism law combining punitive and preventive elements — primarily security-based.

Value Addition:
• COFEPOSA was upheld as a valid restriction on Article 19(1)(g) (right to trade) on economic security grounds.
• MISA was repealed after the Emergency ended — it is a repealed law but still tested in MCQs.
• State-level 'Goonda Acts' operate under Entry 3 of the Concurrent List — they are the primary state-level preventive detention mechanisms.

solution.concept_anchor: Right to representation — detaining authority vs Advisory Board

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 1: Article 22(5) guarantees the detenu's right to make a representation against the detention order both to the detaining authority and to the Advisory Board, and failure to afford either opportunity independently vitiates the detention.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 22(5) explicitly confers the right to make a representation to the detaining authority. The right to represent before the Advisory Board is a separate judicial expansion — not textually specified as a right in Article 22(5). While failure to afford either vitiates detention, the grouping of both as explicit Article 22(5) rights is an overstatement.

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 2: Article 22 does not explicitly guarantee the right to legal representation before the Advisory Board — the Supreme Court in A.K. Roy v. Union of India (1982) held that a detenu does not have an absolute constitutional right to a lawyer before the Advisory Board.
statement_analysis.reason: This is precisely what A.K. Roy (1982) held — the right to legal representation before the Advisory Board is not an absolute constitutional right under Article 22; it may be granted or denied by statute.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because both statements deal with the right to representation, and students who recall that both rights 'vitiates detention if violated' assume both statements are correct without scrutinising the textual basis of Statement 1.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Article 22(5) explicitly gives the right to represent only to the detaining authority — the right to represent before the Advisory Board is a judicial expansion, not textually part of 22(5). The phrase 'both to the detaining authority and to the Advisory Board' overstates the textual provision, making Statement 1 incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: A.K. Roy v. Union of India (1982) is a real and correctly cited judgment — it held no absolute right to legal representation before Advisory Board. Statement 2 is correct.
Statement 1 incorrect + Statement 2 correct → select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 combines two true facts — that failure to afford representation to the detaining authority vitiates detention AND that failure to afford representation before the Advisory Board also vitiates detention — into a statement that attributes both rights directly to Article 22(5)'s text. The trap is that Article 22(5) only textually provides for representation to the detaining authority; the right to represent before the Advisory Board is a judicial gloss. Combining both under a single textual provision makes Statement 1 partially false.
solution.final_explanation:
The right to make a representation is a critical safeguard under Article 22(5). However, its textual scope and judicially expanded scope must be distinguished.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Article 22(5) textually provides the right to make a representation to the detaining authority. The right to represent before the Advisory Board is a separate right developed through judicial interpretation — it is not explicitly stated as part of Article 22(5)'s text. Conflating both as Article 22(5) rights overstates the textual provision.
• Statement 2 — Correct: A.K. Roy v. Union of India (1982) explicitly held that the detenu does not have an absolute constitutional right to legal representation before the Advisory Board. Some statutes (like COFEPOSA) grant this as a statutory right, but it is not a constitutional guarantee.

Value Addition:
• Undue delay in considering the detenu's representation vitiates continued detention — the Supreme Court has read promptness into the Article 22(5) obligation.
• Representation must be considered by the appropriate authority — if routed incorrectly, it can be a procedural ground for release.
• The distinction between constitutional rights and statutory rights in the context of Advisory Board proceedings is a recurring UPSC theme.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 22(7) — exclusive Parliamentary power for extended detention
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is deceptive because students who recall that both Parliament and State Legislatures can make preventive detention laws (Entry 3, Concurrent List) assume the same parity applies to the Article 22(7) override.
elimination_logic: Identify the blank context: Article 22(7) deals with prescribing circumstances for detention beyond 3 months without Advisory Board — this is a constitutional override.
Eliminate (a): The President does not legislate — Article 22(7) empowers the legislature to prescribe by law.
Eliminate (b): The Supreme Court does not legislate — judicial bodies have no role in prescribing detention periods.
Eliminate (d): State Legislatures are explicitly excluded from invoking Article 22(7) — this power is exclusive to Parliament.
Confirm (c): Article 22(7) explicitly empowers Parliament alone to prescribe by law the circumstances and maximum period of detention without Advisory Board reference.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap in option (d) is highly effective because students correctly know that State Legislatures can make preventive detention laws under Entry 3 of the Concurrent List. They then incorrectly extend this to Article 22(7) — assuming that if States can legislate on preventive detention generally, they can also invoke the Article 22(7) override. But Article 22(7) is an exclusive Parliamentary power that cannot be delegated to or exercised by State Legislatures.
solution.final_explanation:

Under Article 22(4), detention beyond 3 months generally requires an Advisory Board opinion. Article 22(7) creates an override: by law, ________ may prescribe circumstances under which this Advisory Board requirement can be bypassed.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The President has executive, not legislative, power — Article 22(7) requires prescribing 'by law,' which is a legislative function.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The Supreme Court is a judicial body with no law-making power under Article 22(7).
• Option (c) — Correct: Article 22(7) vests this extraordinary power exclusively in Parliament. No state legislature, no executive order — only an Act of Parliament can invoke it.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: State Legislatures can make preventive detention laws but cannot invoke Article 22(7)'s specific override — this federal distinction is constitutionally explicit.

Value Addition:
• Parliament has not yet enacted comprehensive legislation exercising its full Article 22(7) power — it remains constitutionally dormant.
• TADA and POTA extended detention periods using a combination of Article 22(7) principles and other entries — but were not enacted solely under Article 22(7).
• The 44th Amendment sought to reduce the 3-month default but was never brought into force.

concepts_used: Doctrine of Sufficient Cause and Subjective Satisfaction in Preventive Detention

solution.concept_anchor: Subjective satisfaction in preventive detention — reviewable limits
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because 'stale grounds vitiate detention' is true, but pairing it with 'only if the detenu proves mala fides' adds a false condition — courts invalidate stale grounds even without proven mala fides.
elimination_logic: Evaluate (a): Subjective satisfaction does not mean unreviewable — courts examine application of mind, relevance of grounds, and procedural compliance. The claim that it means 'courts cannot examine the detention in any manner' is a false scope extension. Incorrect pair.

Evaluate (b): Stale grounds do vitiate detention, but courts do not require the detenu to 'prove mala fides' — the causal link between grounds and detention order must appear on the face of the record. The added condition makes this incorrect.

Evaluate (c): Courts CAN review whether the Advisory Board was properly constituted and followed procedure — but cannot substitute their opinion on the sufficiency of cause. The pair says courts 'cannot review any aspect' which is a false scope extension. Incorrect.

Evaluate (d): Correctly states that judicial review examines reasonableness of grounds and procedural compliance — not the merits of the detention decision itself. This is the accurately stated principle. Correct pair.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) exploits the common belief that 'subjective satisfaction' means nearly absolute executive discretion. Option (c) exploits the partial truth that courts show deference to the Advisory Board — but 'cannot review any aspect' is a false scope extension. The correct answer (d) precisely captures the distinction: judicial review is permissible on procedure and relevance of grounds, but not on whether the executive was right to detain.
solution.final_explanation:
Subjective satisfaction is the cornerstone of preventive detention — the detaining authority acts on its own assessment of necessity, and courts do not second-guess that assessment on its merits. However, subjective satisfaction is not a blank cheque.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Subjective satisfaction does not immunise the order from all judicial scrutiny. Courts examine: (i) whether the authority applied its mind, (ii) whether grounds are relevant and non-vague, and (iii) whether mala fides or non-application of mind is evident.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Stale grounds vitiate detention without requiring proof of mala fides — the temporal disconnect between the grounds and the detention order itself breaks the causal link.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Courts CAN review whether the Advisory Board was properly constituted and followed prescribed procedure — they only refrain from substituting their opinion on the sufficiency of cause.
• Option (d) — Correct: This accurately states the judicial review standard — reasonableness of grounds and procedural compliance are reviewable; the merits of the detention decision itself are not.

Value Addition:
• 'Stale cause' doctrine: If the event giving rise to detention was months or years old, the detention order lacks the requisite proximity.
• Mala fides, if proved, is an independent ground to vitiate a detention order.
• Vague grounds that do not enable the detenu to make an effective representation are a classic procedural ground for quashing.

concepts_used: Preventive Detention During National Emergency — Articles 358 and 359 Interface

solution.concept_anchor: Emergency — Article 358/359 and Article 22 interface; ADM Jabalpur overruling

statement_analysis.statement: During a National Emergency under Article 352, Article 358 automatically suspends the operation of Article 19 rights — thereby removing one layer of challenge to preventive detention laws.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 358 suspends Article 19 rights for the duration of a National Emergency — this removes the Article 19 challenge to preventive detention laws, leaving only Articles 21 and 22 as possible checks.

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 359, the President may suspend the right to move courts for enforcement of all fundamental rights including Articles 20 and 21 during a National Emergency.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 359 allows suspension of enforcement of most fundamental rights, but Articles 20 and 21 are explicitly excluded — they are always enforceable even during a National Emergency.

statement_analysis.statement: The Supreme Court in K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) overruled ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla (1976), holding that Articles 20 and 21 remain enforceable even when Article 359 is in operation.
statement_analysis.reason: Puttaswamy (2017) explicitly overruled ADM Jabalpur (1976) on this point — confirming that Articles 20 and 21 are not suspendable under Article 359 and are always available to challenge detention.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) '1 and 3 only' is the correct answer but students who confuse Article 358 (automatic) with Article 359 (Presidential order) or mistakenly believe ADM Jabalpur was never overruled will select 'd' (all three).
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Article 358 automatically suspends Article 19 during National Emergency — this is constitutionally correct. Statement 1 is correct.

Statement 2: Article 359 explicitly CANNOT suspend Articles 20 and 21 — the statement that 'all fundamental rights including Articles 20 and 21' can be suspended is factually wrong. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 3: Puttaswamy (2017) did overrule ADM Jabalpur and confirmed the permanent enforceability of Articles 20 and 21. Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct — select option (c): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the critical trap. Many students who have studied Emergency provisions recall that 'Article 359 allows suspension of fundamental rights during Emergency' and miss the crucial exception: Articles 20 and 21 are explicitly excluded by the Constitution (after the 44th Amendment). The ADM Jabalpur case controversially held that Article 21 could be suspended — Puttaswamy definitively overruled this, making Statement 3's content exam-critical.
solution.final_explanation:
The intersection of Emergency provisions and preventive detention requires precision about Articles 358 and 359.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 358 is automatic — the moment National Emergency is proclaimed, Article 19 rights stand suspended. This removes the Article 19(1)(d)/(e) challenge to preventive detention laws restricting movement.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 359 empowers the President to suspend enforcement of fundamental rights by court order — but the 44th Amendment (1978) carved out Articles 20 and 21 permanently from this suspension power. They remain enforceable even during Emergency. The statement's claim that 'all fundamental rights including 20 and 21' can be suspended is constitutionally wrong.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Puttaswamy (2017) formally overruled ADM Jabalpur — confirming that the right to life (Article 21) and protection against ex post facto laws (Article 20) are non-derogable under any provision.

Value Addition:
• Article 358 operates automatically; Article 359 requires a Presidential Order specifying which rights are suspended.
• The 44th Amendment's exclusion of Articles 20 and 21 from Article 359 suspension was a direct legislative response to ADM Jabalpur's excesses.
• During Emergency, Article 22 procedural safeguards technically remain unless specifically addressed by law — but weakened judicial oversight is a practical concern.

concepts_used: Successive Detention Orders: Constitutional Permissibility and Judicial Scrutiny

solution.concept_anchor: Successive detention — fresh grounds required, recycled grounds invalid
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is deceptive because it sounds like a principled constitutional position — that quashing creates a bar similar to res judicata — when in fact a fresh order with genuinely new grounds IS permissible.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Successive detention is not unconstitutional per se — the Constitution permits fresh detention orders if fresh grounds exist.
Eliminate (c): Quashing a detention order does not permanently bar re-detention — it only bars reiteration of the same invalid grounds, not genuinely new ones.
Eliminate (d): Courts do not require legislative authorisation for each successive detention — the executive can issue fresh orders under existing law on new grounds.

Confirm (b): A fresh detention order can follow a quashed one — but only if it rests on genuinely independent new grounds. Recycling invalidated grounds will cause the new order to be struck down as well.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (c) fabricates a 'permanent bar' rule that sounds constitutionally principled — after all, res judicata prevents re-litigation of decided matters. Students who extrapolate from this principle assume quashing creates a permanent barrier. The correct position is narrower: only the recycled grounds are barred — the executive can detain again if it has new, independent grounds.
solution.final_explanation:
Successive detention orders occupy an interesting space in preventive detention law — they are constitutionally permissible, subject to a critical condition.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Successive detention is not constitutionally prohibited. Fresh detention orders are valid if premised on independent grounds.
• Option (b) — Correct: This is the Haradhan Saha principle — each detention order must stand on its own independent grounds. A fresh order that merely reiterates grounds already declared invalid will be struck down, as courts will see through the attempt to circumvent the earlier judicial order.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: There is no absolute permanent bar on re-detention after quashing. The bar is specifically against recycling invalidated grounds — genuinely new grounds permit fresh detention.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: No separate legislative authorisation is required for each successive order — the executive acts under existing detention law.

Value Addition:
• This principle functions as a functional anti-circumvention safeguard — executives cannot play 'whack-a-mole' with courts by repeatedly reissuing orders.
• Courts look at the substance of the grounds, not just their formal presentation, to determine if they are genuinely new.
• The Haradhan Saha principle also applies to ensure grounds are proximate and not stale at the time of the fresh order.

Rights of Arrested Persons Under Article 22(1) and 22(2)

solution.concept_anchor: Legal representation — ordinary arrest vs Advisory Board — constitutional vs statutory right

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 1: The right to consult a legal practitioner of one's choice under Article 22(1) applies at the time of ordinary arrest and extends to all subsequent stages of legal proceedings, including appearances before the Advisory Board in preventive detention cases.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 22(1)'s right to consult a lawyer applies at the stage of ordinary arrest — it does not extend to or apply before the Advisory Board in preventive detention proceedings, which are governed by Article 22(4)–(7).

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 2: In A.K. Roy v. Union of India (1982), the Supreme Court held that a preventive detenu does not have an absolute constitutional right to be represented by a lawyer before the Advisory Board, and statutes may permit or deny such representation.
statement_analysis.reason: A.K. Roy (1982) is correctly cited — the Court held that Article 22 does not guarantee an absolute right to legal representation before the Advisory Board; it is a statutory right where the relevant law provides for it.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because both statements deal with legal representation rights — students familiar with both provisions may assume both are correct without carefully tracing the scope of Article 22(1).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Article 22(1)'s lawyer-consultation right is for ordinary arrest — it does not textually or judicially extend to Advisory Board proceedings in preventive detention. The extension claimed in Statement 1 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: A.K. Roy (1982) did hold exactly what Statement 2 says — no absolute constitutional right to a lawyer before Advisory Board. Statement 2 is correct.
Statement 1 incorrect + Statement 2 correct → select option (d).

Wait — re-check option mapping: (c) says 'Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect'; (d) says 'Statement 1 incorrect, Statement 2 correct.' Since Statement 2 is correct and Statement 1 is incorrect, the correct option is (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 conflates two legally distinct contexts: the right to consult a lawyer at the time of arrest under Article 22(1), and representation before the Advisory Board in preventive detention. Students who know the general principle that 'Article 22 gives the right to a lawyer' apply it across all stages without recognising the structural bifurcation of Article 22 — the ordinary arrest rights do not migrate into the preventive detention regime.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 22 bifurcates legal representation rights across its two distinct regimes.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Article 22(1) guarantees the right to consult a lawyer at the time of ordinary arrest. This right is specific to the ordinary arrest regime (Articles 22(1)&(2)) and does NOT extend to Advisory Board proceedings in preventive detention. The two regimes are separate — a person detained under preventive detention cannot invoke Article 22(1)'s lawyer right for Advisory Board appearances.
• Statement 2 — Correct: A.K. Roy v. Union of India (1982) squarely held that no absolute constitutional right to legal representation before the Advisory Board exists under Article 22. COFEPOSA, for instance, permits such representation — making it a statutory right in that context. But constitutionally, it is not guaranteed.

Value Addition:
• The reason for excluding lawyers from Advisory Board proceedings has been justified on the ground that the Board's proceedings are investigative/quasi-judicial, not adversarial.
• This remains a contested area — critics argue that denying lawyers before the Advisory Board undermines the quality of the detenu's representation.
• Statutory right vs constitutional right is a recurring MCQ distinction in UPSC.

solution.concept_anchor: TADA/POTA/UAPA — constitutional entries and Article 22 compliance

statement_analysis.statement: TADA and POTA, which permitted extended custody periods of up to 180 days, were justified directly under Article 22(7) of the Constitution as laws prescribing detention beyond the standard 3-month Advisory Board threshold.
statement_analysis.reason: TADA and POTA operated under Entry 1 (Defence) and Entry 9 (Union List) — they were not enacted solely or directly under Article 22(7). They still had to comply with Article 22's minimum safeguards even while extending detention periods.

statement_analysis.statement: The Supreme Court in Kartar Singh v. State of Punjab (1994) upheld TADA in its entirety without reading down any of its provisions.
statement_analysis.reason: In Kartar Singh (1994), the Supreme Court upheld TADA but read down certain provisions — it did not uphold the entire statute without qualification. The case illustrates that even special laws remain subject to Article 22 review.

statement_analysis.statement: Special laws such as UAPA 2019 (as amended) must still comply with the minimum procedural safeguards prescribed under Article 22, even though they operate under Union List entries.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 22's minimum safeguards are not waivable by Parliament merely because a law operates under Union List entries — all preventive detention laws must comply with Article 22's procedural floor, regardless of the legislative entry under which they are enacted.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) '1 only' is deceptive because Statement 1 appears technically correct to students who associate Article 22(7) with extended detention periods and assume TADA/POTA invoked it.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: TADA and POTA were justified under Union List entries (Entry 1 and Entry 9), not directly under Article 22(7) — the claim that they were 'justified directly under Article 22(7)' is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: Kartar Singh (1994) upheld TADA but READ DOWN certain provisions — the claim 'upheld in its entirety without reading down' is factually wrong. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: All preventive detention laws must comply with Article 22 minimum safeguards — this is correct regardless of the legislative entry.
Statements 1 and 2 are NOT correct — select option (b): 1 and 2.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits the association between extended detention periods and Article 22(7) — students assume that since TADA extended detention beyond 3 months, it must have invoked Article 22(7). But TADA and POTA operated under Union List entries and had to comply with Article 22's safeguards independently — they were not 'direct' Article 22(7) enactments. Statement 2 tests precision about Kartar Singh — 'read down' and 'upheld entirely' are different legal outcomes.
solution.final_explanation:
Special security legislations in India have repeatedly tested the outer limits of Article 22.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: TADA (repealed 1995) and POTA (repealed 2004) derived their legislative authority from Union List entries (particularly Entries 1 and 9) — not from Article 22(7) directly. Article 22(7) has never been fully operationalised by Parliament as a standalone basis for extended detention legislation.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: In Kartar Singh v. State of Punjab (1994), the Supreme Court upheld TADA's constitutional validity but specifically READ DOWN certain provisions (such as admissibility of confessions before police officers) — it was not an unqualified validation.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The minimum procedural safeguards in Article 22 function as a constitutional floor — no Parliamentary legislation, regardless of the entry it operates under, can strip away these minimum guarantees.

Value Addition:
• UAPA 2019 amendments allow designation of individuals as terrorists — this individual designation power raises Article 22 and Article 14 concerns distinct from organisational proscription.
• POTA's repeal in 2004 was partly driven by documented abuse of preventive detention provisions.
• 'Reading down' is a constitutional interpretation technique where courts narrow the scope of a provision to save it from unconstitutionality.

solution.concept_anchor: NSA 1980 — procedural timelines and authority to detain

statement_analysis.statement: Under the National Security Act, 1980, initial detention may be ordered by a District Magistrate or Commissioner of Police without prior approval from the Central or State Government.
statement_analysis.reason: The NSA empowers District Magistrates and Commissioners of Police to issue detention orders independently — the Central/State Government must be informed within 12 days and retains the power to revoke.

statement_analysis.statement: Under the NSA, grounds of detention must be communicated to the detenu within 5 days of detention, extendable to 10–15 days in exceptional circumstances.
statement_analysis.reason: NSA prescribes the 5-day default period for communicating grounds, extendable to 10–15 days in cases of exceptional circumstances — this procedural detail is specifically tested in examinations.

statement_analysis.statement: Under the NSA, the Advisory Board must submit its opinion within 10 weeks of the date of detention for the detention to continue beyond 3 months.
statement_analysis.reason: Under NSA rules, the Advisory Board must submit its report within 7 weeks of detention — the 10-week timeline stated here is incorrect.

statement_analysis.statement: The maximum permissible period of detention under the NSA is 12 months from the date of the original detention order.
statement_analysis.reason: NSA permits detention for up to 12 months — initially 3 months, extendable upon Advisory Board confirmation, with the total not exceeding 12 months under a single order.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) 'Only two' is deceptive because students who are uncertain about the 7-week vs 10-week Advisory Board timeline may mark Statement 3 correct, raising their count to four and selecting 'All four' or 'Only three.'
elimination_logic: Statement 1: District Magistrate/Commissioner can order detention without prior government approval under NSA — Correct.
Statement 2: Grounds within 5 days (extendable to 10–15 days) is the NSA-specific procedural requirement — Correct.
Statement 3: Advisory Board must report within 7 weeks, NOT 10 weeks — '10 weeks' is a temporal trap. Incorrect.
Statement 4: Maximum 12 months under NSA — Correct. Three statements are correct → select option (c) 'Only three.'
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Advisory Board timeline — 7 weeks — is a specific numerical detail that students confuse with other timelines (3 months for the basic limit, 12 months for maximum detention). Introducing '10 weeks' as a plausible alternative exploits this confusion. Additionally, the authority to order detention without prior government approval under NSA (Statement 1) is often assumed to require prior sanction by analogy with other laws.
solution.final_explanation:
The National Security Act, 1980 is the principal central preventive detention law for security-related detention and contains several specific procedural timelines.

| Statement | Verdict |
|---|---|
| S1: District Magistrate/Commissioner can order detention without prior approval | Correct |
| S2: Grounds within 5 days (extendable to 10–15 days) | Correct |
| S3: Advisory Board must report within 10 weeks | Incorrect — it is 7 weeks |
| S4: Maximum detention period is 12 months | Correct |

Three statements are correct — 'Only three.'

Value Addition:
• The government must be informed within 12 days of a detention order issued by a District Magistrate/Commissioner — failure to inform within this period vitiates continued detention.
• NSA detention can be for security of India, relations with foreign powers, public order, or maintenance of essential services.
• The 5-day/10–15-day distinction for communicating grounds is an NSA-specific provision — Article 22(5) itself says 'as soon as may be' without specifying days.

solution.concept_anchor: Maneka Gandhi overruling Gopalan — Article 22 not a self-contained code
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students who know both A and R are factually correct assume R must explain A, without verifying the specific causal direction.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. Post-Maneka Gandhi, preventive detention laws must satisfy the triple test of Articles 14, 19, and 21 — Article 22 alone does not insulate them from scrutiny under other fundamental rights.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — No. COFEPOSA was upheld as a valid restriction on Article 19(1)(g) — it was NOT struck down. The statement that COFEPOSA was 'struck down' is factually incorrect.
Step 3: Mismatch identified — A is correct, R is incorrect → select option (c).
Final check: correct_option is (c) — A correct, R incorrect.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Reason claims COFEPOSA was struck down — this is factually wrong. COFEPOSA was upheld by the Supreme Court as a valid restriction on the right to trade under Article 19(1)(g) on economic security grounds. Students who recall that COFEPOSA has faced constitutional challenge may confuse challenge with invalidation. The Assertion is correct (Maneka's triple test applies to preventive detention laws), but the Reason provides a false illustration.
solution.final_explanation:
The post-Maneka Gandhi framework transformed the constitutional scrutiny of preventive detention laws.

• Assertion (A) — Correct: After Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), preventive detention laws cannot be assessed solely under Article 22's procedural safeguards. They must additionally pass the triple test — they must not be arbitrary (Article 14), must not impose unreasonable restrictions on Article 19 freedoms, and must satisfy due process standards under Article 21. Article 22 is not a self-contained code.
• Reason (R) — Incorrect: COFEPOSA was NOT struck down — it was upheld by the Supreme Court as constitutionally valid on the ground that detention to prevent smuggling and conserve foreign exchange constitutes a reasonable restriction on Article 19(1)(g) (right to trade). The Reason incorrectly states that COFEPOSA was struck down.

Since A is correct and R is incorrect → option (c).

Value Addition:
• COFEPOSA remains in force — it is a valid central preventive detention law targeting economic offences.
• The economic security rationale (conservation of foreign exchange) was accepted as sufficient justification for restricting Article 19(1)(g) rights.
• A.K. Gopalan (1950) held the opposite — that Article 22 was a self-contained code. Maneka Gandhi definitively ended this silo approach.

solution.concept_anchor: Procedural non-compliance voids detention — language of grounds
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is deceptive because remanding to the detaining authority sounds like an appropriate corrective measure — students expect courts to give the government a chance to cure the defect rather than immediately ordering release.
elimination_logic: Identify the legal issue: Grounds were communicated only in English; Prabhavati reads only Marathi. This is a procedural violation — communicating grounds in a language the detenu does not understand defeats the right under Article 22(5).
Eliminate (a): The court cannot uphold the detention despite a constitutional violation — procedural compliance under Article 22 is a substantive requirement, not a formality.
Eliminate (c): Remanding to the detaining authority to re-communicate grounds does not cure the original constitutional breach — the detention order is void from the point of the violation.
Eliminate (d): The government cannot unilaterally translate and extend detention — this would require a fresh, valid detention order after the original is struck down.

Confirm (b): Courts consistently order immediate release when Article 22 procedural safeguards are violated — even technical violations like communicating grounds in an unknown language render detention void, not merely voidable.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 22(5) requires that grounds of detention be communicated to the detenu — but judicial interpretation has extended this to require communication in a language the detenu understands. This is not a technicality but a substantive constitutional requirement: the purpose of communicating grounds is to enable the detenu to make an effective representation. If the grounds are in a language the detenu cannot read, the constitutional purpose is defeated.

Consequence: The detention order is void (not merely voidable) — courts will order immediate release under habeas corpus.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Constitutional procedural violations cannot be overlooked — the court cannot uphold the detention despite the violation.
• Option (b) — Correct: Immediate release through habeas corpus is the appropriate remedy — the violation renders the detention order void.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: A remand to re-communicate grounds does not retrospectively cure the void detention — a fresh detention order with proper procedure would be needed.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Unilateral translation by the government while keeping the detention in force is not constitutionally permissible — the taint on the original order cannot be cured this way.

Value Addition:
• Communication in an unknown language has been judicially equated to non-communication — both defeat Article 22(5)'s purpose.
• Void vs voidable distinction: A void order has no legal effect from inception; a voidable order requires a court to set it aside.
• Habeas corpus under Article 226 (High Court) is typically the first port of call — speedier than Article 32.

solution.concept_anchor: Gopalan Section 14 struck down — even within upholding the Act
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students who know Gopalan upheld the Preventive Detention Act assume the entire Act was upheld without nuance — missing the specific section struck down.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): The Supreme Court in Gopalan did NOT uphold the entire Preventive Detention Act 1950 — it struck down Section 14 which prohibited disclosure of grounds.
Eliminate (b): Gopalan did not overrule anything — it established the silo theory; overruling came much later in Maneka Gandhi.
Eliminate (d): Gopalan did not hold that preventive detention was unconstitutional — it upheld the Act's broad constitutionality.

Confirm (c): Gopalan struck down Section 14 of the Preventive Detention Act which prohibited courts from examining grounds of detention — establishing the principle that even while upholding a detention law, specific provisions can be invalidated.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students who recall 'Gopalan upheld preventive detention' assume the Act was upheld wholesale. The nuance — that Section 14 (prohibiting disclosure of grounds) was struck down even in Gopalan — is a critical detail. This demonstrates the early judicial assertion that not all provisions of a detention law are insulated from scrutiny, even before Maneka Gandhi's broader framework.
solution.final_explanation:
A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950) was the Supreme Court's first major engagement with preventive detention and the Preventive Detention Act, 1950.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Court did not uphold the entire Act. It upheld the broad constitutionality of preventive detention but struck down Section 14 — the provision that prohibited courts from examining or disclosing the grounds of detention.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Gopalan did not overrule any earlier precedent on fundamental rights — it established the silo theory for the first time.
• Option (c) — Correct: Section 14 of the Preventive Detention Act, which barred the detenu from disclosing grounds to a court and prohibited courts from examining them, was struck down in Gopalan. This was a foundational early assertion of judicial review over detention law provisions.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Gopalan upheld preventive detention as constitutionally permissible — it did not invalidate it.

Value Addition:
• The silo theory from Gopalan: each fundamental right operates independently — Articles 14, 19, 21 cannot be read together to challenge a detention law.
• Maneka Gandhi (1978) definitively overruled the silo theory.
• Gopalan's judicial significance: even while deferring to the legislature, the Court drew a line at total non-disclosure — a foundational anti-suppression principle.

Students who know both entries exist but are uncertain of their precise location in the Lists will be tempted by option (b), which reverses the two. Understanding the distribution of legislative competence over preventive detention is essential for UPSC.

• The Concurrent List character of Entry 3 means State Goonda Acts are valid — they draw their authority from Entry 3.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) '1950' is deceptive because students associate 1950 with A.K. Gopalan — the foundational preventive detention case — and may confuse the year of the overruling case with the overruled case.
elimination_logic: Identify the blank: The question asks for the year in which the Supreme Court in Maneka Gandhi overruled the Gopalan silo theory.
Eliminate (c): 1976 is the year of ADM Jabalpur — not Maneka Gandhi.
Eliminate (d): 1950 is the year of A.K. Gopalan — the case being overruled, not the one doing the overruling.
Eliminate (a): 1967 is associated with Golaknath v. State of Punjab (Parliament's power to amend fundamental rights) — unrelated to the silo theory.
Confirm (b): Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India was decided in 1978 — the year the silo theory was overruled and the triple-test framework established.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The 1950 option targets students who recall that Gopalan established the silo theory — they associate 1950 with the doctrine and may misread the blank as asking for when the silo theory was established rather than when it was overruled. The 1976 option targets students who conflate Maneka Gandhi with the Emergency-era ADM Jabalpur judgment, which also dealt with personal liberty but reached the opposite conclusion.
solution.final_explanation:
The silo theory — that each fundamental right operates independently and courts cannot read Articles 14, 19, and 21 together to challenge a law — was established in A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950) and definitively overruled in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India in ________ (1978).

• Option (a) — 1967 — Incorrect: This year is associated with Golaknath v. State of Punjab, which concerned Parliament's power to amend fundamental rights — unrelated to the silo theory.
• Option (b) — 1978 — Correct: Maneka Gandhi was decided in 1978 — the Supreme Court held that Articles 14, 19, and 21 must be read together, overruling the isolation principle.
• Option (c) — 1976 — Incorrect: ADM Jabalpur (1976) actually reinforced executive power over detention during the Emergency — it was later overruled by Puttaswamy (2017), not related to the silo theory.
• Option (d) — 1950 — Incorrect: This is the year Gopalan established the silo theory — not when it was overruled.

Value Addition:
• Maneka Gandhi's triple test: a law depriving life or liberty must satisfy Articles 14 (non-arbitrariness), 19 (reasonable restriction), and 21 (fair, just, and reasonable procedure).
• Maneka Gandhi is one of the most cited judgments in Indian constitutional law.
• Justice P.N. Bhagwati's opinion in Maneka Gandhi expanded the meaning of 'procedure established by law' to include substantive due process.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 22 protections — who gets them, who does not

statement_analysis.statement: A person detained under a preventive detention law cannot invoke the rights under Article 22(1) to consult a lawyer of their choice or Article 22(2) to be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 22(3)(b) explicitly excludes persons arrested under preventive detention laws from the protections of Article 22(1) and (2) — these rights belong only to the ordinary arrest regime.

statement_analysis.statement: Enemy aliens, being excluded from Article 22(1) and (2), are instead governed by the preventive detention safeguards under Article 22(4)–(7) whenever detained.
statement_analysis.reason: Enemy aliens are excluded from BOTH regimes under Article 22 — neither the ordinary arrest rights (22(1)&(2)) nor the preventive detention safeguards (22(4)–(7)) apply to them as a constitutional matter.

statement_analysis.statement: A foreign national from a country not at war with India, who is arrested on suspicion of committing a criminal offence, is entitled to the protections under Article 22(1) and (2).
statement_analysis.reason: Article 22(3) excludes only 'enemy aliens' — foreign nationals from friendly or neutral countries are not enemy aliens and therefore retain the full Article 22(1) and (2) protections upon ordinary arrest.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) '1 and 3 only' IS the correct answer but option (d) '1, 2 and 3' is the strong distractor — students who recall that enemy aliens are excluded from 22(1)&(2) may assume they must fall under the only other available regime (22(4)–(7)), making Statement 2 appear correct.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Article 22(3)(b) explicitly removes Article 22(1)&(2) protections from preventive detenues — Correct.
Statement 2: Enemy aliens lose BOTH sets of protections — the claim they are 'governed by 22(4)–(7)' is wrong. Incorrect.
Statement 3: Only enemy aliens (nationals of countries at war with India) are excluded — friendly foreign nationals retain 22(1)&(2) rights. Correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct → select option (a): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the trap — it is logically seductive to assume that if enemy aliens lose one protection, they must get the other. The Constitution creates a total exclusion for enemy aliens from all Article 22 protections — they fall into a constitutionally sanctioned rights-free zone under Article 22. This is one of the most counterintuitive provisions in the entire chapter on fundamental rights.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 22(3) creates two exclusions from the ordinary arrest protections: enemy aliens and preventive detenues.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 22(3)(b) is unambiguous — persons arrested under preventive detention laws cannot invoke the 24-hour magistrate production rule or the right to consult a lawyer under Article 22(1).
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Enemy aliens are not transferred to the preventive detention protection regime under Article 22(4)–(7). Article 22(3)(a) creates a total exclusion — enemy aliens have no Article 22 rights as a constitutional matter. This is an absolute constitutional exception.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The exclusion applies only to 'enemy aliens.' A foreign national from, say, France or Japan arrested in India on criminal grounds is not an enemy alien and retains full Article 22(1)&(2) protections.

Value Addition:
• 'Enemy alien' status depends on the nationality of the person and whether India is at war with that country — it is a dynamic status, not permanent.
• The constitutional exclusion of enemy aliens from all Article 22 protections has been critiqued as potentially inconsistent with international humanitarian law obligations.
• India's Enemy Aliens Act provides the legislative framework for dealing with enemy aliens in practice.

solution.concept_anchor: Bail vs habeas corpus — distinct remedies in detention law
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because students assume 'right to representation' broadly includes a right to a lawyer at all stages, including before the Advisory Board.
elimination_logic: Evaluate (a): Courts do grant bail in ordinary criminal arrests — but the claim that the same mechanism applies in preventive detention is incorrect (conflation of regimes).

Evaluate (b): Article 22(5) provides the right to make a representation — but this is the right to make a written representation, not the right to legal representation by a counsel. The pair conflates two distinct rights.
Evaluate (c): 'No right to bail in preventive detention — relief available only through habeas corpus or revocation by detaining authority' — this correctly states the principle. Correctly matched.

Evaluate (d): Article 22(5)'s representation right is to the detaining authority — not specifically to the Advisory Board (that is a judicially expanded right). The pair incorrectly characterises the textual basis.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) conflates the right to make a written representation under Article 22(5) with the right to legal representation by a counsel. These are fundamentally different: the first is a personal right to submit a written statement opposing detention; the second is the right to have an advocate appear on your behalf. A.K. Roy (1982) confirmed that the latter is not a constitutional right before the Advisory Board.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests precision in distinguishing related but legally distinct concepts in preventive detention law.

• Option (a) — Incorrectly matched: Bail on merits is the remedy in ordinary criminal cases — in preventive detention, there is no right to bail. Courts cannot grant bail in preventive detention cases the way they do in criminal matters.
• Option (b) — Incorrectly matched: Article 22(5) confers the right to make a personal representation (a written submission opposing detention) — not the right to be represented by a lawyer. These are different rights; the latter is not constitutionally guaranteed before the Advisory Board.
• Option (c) — Correctly matched: In preventive detention, the proper judicial remedy is habeas corpus. If the court finds the order void, it orders release — which is functionally similar to bail but is legally a different mechanism. The detaining authority can also revoke the order independently.
• Option (d) — Incorrectly matched: Article 22(5)'s textual right to make a representation is to the detaining authority — the right to represent before the Advisory Board is a judicially expanded right, not the primary textual obligation under 22(5).

Value Addition:
• Revocation by the detaining authority is an administrative remedy distinct from judicial intervention.
• The habeas corpus petition can be filed before the High Court (Article 226) or the Supreme Court (Article 32) — Article 226 is broader in scope.
• Procedural violation → detention void → immediate release through habeas corpus is the complete chain.

solution.concept_anchor: Grounds communication — vagueness, non-disclosure limits, and stale cause

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 22(6), if the detaining authority withholds certain facts on grounds of public interest, the obligation to communicate grounds under Article 22(5) is proportionally reduced — the detenu need only be informed of the non-withheld facts.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 22(5) and 22(6) operate simultaneously — non-disclosure under 22(6) does not reduce the grounds-communication obligation under 22(5). The obligation to communicate sufficient grounds (even if specific sensitive facts are withheld) remains intact.

statement_analysis.statement: Where grounds of detention are vague or irrelevant, the detention order is vitiated because the detenu cannot make an effective representation — this principle was articulated in Haradhan Saha v. State of West Bengal.
statement_analysis.reason: Haradhan Saha is correctly cited for this principle — vague or irrelevant grounds that prevent the detenu from making an effective representation render the detention order invalid.

statement_analysis.statement: Under the 'stale cause' doctrine, a detention order issued more than six months after the events cited as grounds is automatically void regardless of any other circumstances.
statement_analysis.reason: The stale cause doctrine does not operate with a fixed six-month automatic threshold — courts examine whether the causal link between the events and the detention decision remains reasonably proximate, which is a case-by-case assessment, not a rigid temporal formula.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) '2 only' is the correct answer but option (a) '1 only' is a strong distractor — students who correctly identify Statement 1 as wrong may assume Statement 3 is a legitimate articulation of the doctrine.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Non-disclosure under 22(6) does not reduce the 22(5) obligation — both clauses operate simultaneously. The claim of proportional reduction is wrong. Incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: Haradhan Saha did establish that vague/irrelevant grounds vitiate detention — Correct. Not the incorrect statement.
Evaluate Statement 3: The stale cause doctrine has no automatic six-month threshold — proximity is assessed case-by-case. The 'automatic void' formulation is a false scope extension. Incorrect.
Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct → select option (d): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 creates a plausible-sounding automatic rule (six months → automatic void) for the stale cause doctrine. The actual doctrine requires courts to assess whether the causal link between events and the detention order is sufficiently proximate — no rigid six-month or any other fixed-period rule exists in constitutional law. Students who know the doctrine exists but not its precise formulation will accept Statement 3 as a correct articulation.
solution.final_explanation:
The communication of grounds and the doctrine of sufficient cause are intertwined safeguards in preventive detention.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The obligation under Article 22(5) and the non-disclosure power under Article 22(6) co-exist — the authority must communicate sufficient grounds to enable an effective representation, even while withholding specific sensitive facts. Non-disclosure under 22(6) is not a licence to reduce the grounds communicated under 22(5).
• Statement 2 — Correct: Haradhan Saha v. State of WB established the principle that grounds must be sufficient and specific enough to enable the detenu to make an effective representation — vague or irrelevant grounds vitiate the order.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The stale cause doctrine has no automatic six-month threshold. Courts examine whether the events cited are sufficiently proximate to justify the detention order — this is a contextual, case-by-case standard, not a bright-line temporal rule.

Value Addition:
• The phrase 'as soon as may be' in Article 22(5) has been judicially read to mean 'at the earliest practicable moment' — not immediately, but without unnecessary delay.
• A total non-disclosure of ALL grounds — even on public interest grounds — is constitutionally impermissible.
• The proximity test in stale cause doctrine: the closer in time the events are to the detention order, the stronger the causal link.
