solution.concept_anchor: Advisory Board quasi-judicial character — courts review constitution and procedure
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because both A and R are individually correct and the relationship between them appears obvious — students who do not check the precise causal direction select (a) without further analysis.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. Courts can review whether the Advisory Board was properly constituted and whether it followed the prescribed procedure — but they cannot substitute their opinion on whether there was 'sufficient cause' for continued detention.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. The Advisory Board must be composed of persons who are, or have been, or are qualified to be High Court judges — this ensures a quasi-judicial character, not a judicial one.

Step 3: Does R explain A? — No. The quasi-judicial composition of the Board (R) does not causally explain why courts limit their review to constitution and procedure (A). The review limitation flows from the constitutional design that vests assessment of 'sufficient cause' in the Board, not from the Board's composition. Both are correct facts but the causal connection is absent.
Both A and R correct, R does NOT explain A → select option (b).
solution.final_explanation:
The Advisory Board occupies a unique constitutional space — it is quasi-judicial but not a court, and the degree to which courts can review its proceedings is carefully calibrated.

• Assertion (A) — Correct: Courts in habeas corpus proceedings can examine: (i) whether the Advisory Board was properly constituted (composition satisfies Article 22's requirement), and (ii) whether it followed the prescribed procedure. However, courts cannot assess whether the Board was right in finding 'sufficient cause' — that assessment is vested in the Board alone.
• Reason (R) — Correct: The constitutional requirement that Board members be qualified as High Court judges is accurate — it is the mechanism that ensures the quasi-judicial character of the proceedings.
• Causal link — Absent: R describes the Board's composition; A describes the scope of judicial review. The limited scope of judicial review (A) flows from the constitutional design choice to vest sufficiency-of-cause assessment in the Board — not from the fact that Board members are qualified judges. Two true facts, no causal connection.

Value Addition:
• If the Advisory Board is constituted with an ineligible member (say, a person not qualified as a High Court judge), courts can and do strike down the continued detention.
• Procedural irregularity in Advisory Board proceedings — e.g., detenu not given opportunity to be heard — is also a ground for judicial intervention.
• The Advisory Board cannot extend detention on its own — it only gives an opinion; the government must act on it.

elimination_logic: Identify the shared attribute: Three of the four options are procedural violations that render a detention order void.
Evaluate (a): Communicating grounds in a language the detenu cannot read defeats the purpose of Article 22(5) — voids the order.

Evaluate (b): The government is NOT constitutionally required to disclose the Advisory Board's opinion to the detenu — the Board's report informs the government's decision; non-disclosure of the report to the detenu is not itself a constitutional violation that voids detention.
Evaluate (c): Undue delay in referring the case to the Advisory Board violates the 3-month procedural timeline under Article 22(4) — voids continued detention.
Evaluate (d): Ignoring the detenu's representation without consideration violates Article 22(5)'s right to make representation — voids continued detention. Option (b) is the odd one out.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (c) and option (b) both deal with the Advisory Board, making one look like a procedural violation that mirrors the other. The critical distinction: delay in referring to the Advisory Board (option c) violates a constitutional timeline; not disclosing the Advisory Board's opinion to the detenu (option b) is not a constitutional requirement — the government uses the Advisory Board's report for its own decision-making, and the Constitution does not require it to be shared with the detenu.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 22's procedural safeguards are substantive constitutional rights — violations typically render detention void. However, not every step in the detention process is constitutionally mandated to be shared with the detenu.

• Option (a): Grounds in an unreadable language defeat the Article 22(5) purpose → voids detention. This IS a void-causing violation.
• Option (b): The Advisory Board submits its opinion/report to the government — there is no constitutional requirement to disclose this report to the detenu. Non-disclosure of the Advisory Board's opinion to the detenu is NOT itself a constitutional violation that voids the detention order. This is the odd one out.
• Option (c): Failure to refer the detention to the Advisory Board within the 3-month period violates Article 22(4)'s mandatory timeline → voids continued detention. This IS a void-causing violation.
• Option (d): Failing to consider the detenu's representation violates Article 22(5)'s right to make an effective representation → voids continued detention. This IS a void-causing violation.

Value Addition:
• The Advisory Board's proceedings are not adversarial — the government does not formally argue against the detenu before the Board.
• Communication of the Board's findings to the detenu may be granted by statute in some cases but is not constitutionally mandated.
• The government can confirm, modify, or revoke detention after receiving the Advisory Board's report.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The TADA timing is the key trap — TADA was enacted in 1985 (not in the 1970s as students sometimes assume because of its association with the Emergency period in memory). UAPA was originally enacted in 1967 but became the primary counter-terrorism law after POTA's repeal in 2004, with significant amendments in 2008 and 2019. solution.final_explanation:
India's special security and preventive detention legislation has evolved over decades, with each law responding to specific security contexts.

Correct sequence: COFEPOSA (1974) → TADA (1985, repealed 1995) → POTA (2002, repealed 2004) → UAPA major amendments (2008, 2019).

• COFEPOSA (1974): Economic security — conservation of foreign exchange and prevention of smuggling.
• TADA (1985): Targeted terrorism and disruptive activities — extended detention up to 1 year; repealed in 1995 after widespread criticism.
• POTA (2002): Post-Parliament attack counter-terrorism law; repealed in 2004; allowed extended custody up to 180 days.
• UAPA (1967, major amendments 2004/2008/2019): Current primary counter-terrorism framework — 2019 amendments added individual terrorist designation power.

Value Addition:
• TADA was the first Indian law to introduce the concept of designated courts for terrorism trials.
• POTA's repeal was partly a political decision by the UPA government in 2004 — but UAPA was simultaneously strengthened.
• Kartar Singh v. State of Punjab (1994) upheld TADA's constitutional validity while reading down specific provisions — a landmark on special security laws and Article 22.

solution.concept_anchor: A.K. Roy 1982 — no absolute right to lawyer before Advisory Board

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 1: The Supreme Court in A.K. Roy v. Union of India (1982) held that a preventive detenu has an absolute constitutional right to be represented by a legal practitioner before the Advisory Board, irrespective of what the relevant statute provides.
statement_analysis.reason: A.K. Roy (1982) held the opposite — the detenu does NOT have an absolute constitutional right to legal representation before the Advisory Board; the statute may permit or disallow it.

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 2: While Article 22 does not explicitly guarantee legal representation before the Advisory Board, some statutes — such as COFEPOSA — do permit such representation, making it a statutory right in those cases.
statement_analysis.reason: This correctly captures the distinction — the right to legal representation before the Advisory Board is statutory, not constitutional, and exists where the relevant law expressly provides for it, as COFEPOSA does.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because both statements deal with legal representation before the Advisory Board, and students who haven't read A.K. Roy precisely may assume both are factually in agreement.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: A.K. Roy (1982) held there is NO absolute constitutional right to a lawyer before the Advisory Board — the statement says the opposite. Statement 1 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: COFEPOSA does permit legal representation before the Advisory Board as a statutory right — this is correctly stated. Statement 2 is correct.
Statement 1 incorrect + Statement 2 correct → select option (d).

Re-check option mapping: (c) = 'Statement 1 correct but Statement 2 incorrect'; (d) = 'Statement 1 incorrect but Statement 2 correct.' Since Statement 1 is wrong and Statement 2 is right, the answer is (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 inverts the A.K. Roy holding — it states the exact opposite of what the case decided. Students who know A.K. Roy dealt with legal representation before the Advisory Board but are uncertain of the precise holding will gravitate toward a statement that 'sounds like a constitutional right' — after all, the right to a lawyer is generally viewed as a fundamental protection. The inversion of the actual holding is the entity-swap trap.
solution.final_explanation:
A.K. Roy v. Union of India (1982) is the definitive pronouncement on legal representation before the Advisory Board.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: A.K. Roy held that a preventive detenu does NOT have an absolute constitutional right to legal representation before the Advisory Board. The detaining law may allow or deny a lawyer — this is within legislative competence, not a constitutional mandate. The statement's assertion of an 'absolute constitutional right' directly contradicts the judgment.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The distinction between constitutional and statutory rights is precisely captured here. COFEPOSA permits legal representation before the Advisory Board — making it a statutory entitlement for persons detained under COFEPOSA, without elevating it to a universal constitutional right.

Value Addition:
• The rationale for denying a mandatory right to a lawyer before the Advisory Board is that the Board's proceedings are investigative rather than adversarial.
• This remains a contested position in legal scholarship — critics argue denial of counsel before a liberty-determining body is a due process concern.
• NSA does not explicitly permit legal representation before the Advisory Board — making COFEPOSA an exception in this regard.

solution.concept_anchor: 44th Amendment, Article 22(7) dormancy, Advisory Board non-binding character

statement_analysis.statement: The 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978) proposed reducing the maximum period of preventive detention without Advisory Board reference from 3 months to 2 months, but this particular provision of the Amendment has not been brought into force.
statement_analysis.reason: This is factually accurate — the 44th Amendment's clause reducing the period to 2 months was passed by Parliament but never notified into operation; the original 3-month rule continues.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 22(7) has been extensively used by Parliament to enact laws prescribing detention beyond 3 months without Advisory Board reference for specified classes of cases.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 22(7) has never been comprehensively operationalised — no Parliament has enacted legislation invoking the full scope of Article 22(7) to prescribe detention beyond 3 months without Advisory Board reference; it remains constitutionally dormant in its pure form.

statement_analysis.statement: Although the Advisory Board under Article 22 must consist of persons qualified to be High Court judges, the government is not constitutionally bound to accept the Board's recommendation — though deviation requires strong justification as interpreted by courts.
statement_analysis.reason: The Advisory Board's report is advisory — the government is not strictly bound to accept it. Courts have held that while deviation is not absolutely barred, it requires strong justification, and the Board's composition requirement (HC-qualified members) ensures quasi-judicial quality.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) '1 and 3 only' is the correct answer but students who believe Article 22(7) has been used (via TADA/POTA) will mark Statement 2 as correct and select 'all three.'
elimination_logic: Statement 1: 44th Amendment's 2-month provision — passed but never notified. Correct.
Statement 2: Article 22(7) has been 'extensively used' — this is factually wrong; it has never been comprehensively operationalised. Incorrect.
Statement 3: Advisory Board opinion is advisory and government is not strictly bound — judicially accepted position. Correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct → select option (d): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the confusion between TADA/POTA's extended detention periods and Article 22(7). Students assume that since these laws extended detention beyond 3 months, Parliament must have been invoking Article 22(7). In reality, TADA and POTA operated under Union List legislative entries — Article 22(7) as a standalone basis for prescribing no-Advisory-Board extended detention has never been comprehensively utilised by Parliament.
solution.final_explanation:
Three distinct but related dimensions of the Advisory Board mechanism and Article 22's legislative framework are tested here.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The 44th Amendment (1978) did propose reducing the 3-month period to 2 months — a response to Emergency-era overreach. However, the relevant provision was never brought into force by executive notification. The Constitution thus still contains the 2-month provision in text, but the 3-month rule operates in practice.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 22(7) represents a constitutionally dormant provision — Parliament has never comprehensively enacted a law prescribing extended detention without Advisory Board reference under Article 22(7)'s framework. TADA and POTA extended detention but operated under different legislative entries, not as pure Article 22(7) exercises.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Advisory Board's opinion is advisory — the government retains final authority on whether to confirm, modify, or revoke detention. Courts have read in a strong justification requirement for deviation, but the government is not formally bound.

Value Addition:
• 'Constitutionally dormant provisions' is an exam concept — provisions that are textually present but operationally inactive (like Article 22(7) in its full scope and several provisions of the 44th Amendment).
• The 44th Amendment also restored habeas corpus protections curtailed during the Emergency.
• Advisory Board decisions are not 'judgments' and cannot be enforced independently — they feed into the government's administrative decision.

solution.concept_anchor: D.K. Basu guidelines — enforceability under Article 21

statement_analysis.statement: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997) held that procedural safeguards elaborated by the Supreme Court for arrested persons — beyond those explicitly listed in Article 22 — are enforceable as part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21.
statement_analysis.reason: D.K. Basu (1997) created a set of custodial guidelines (informing relatives, medical examination, etc.) that go beyond Article 22's text — and the Court held these are enforceable under Article 21 as part of 'procedure established by law' that must be fair, just, and reasonable.

statement_analysis.statement: The D.K. Basu guidelines apply exclusively to cases of preventive detention under special laws and do not govern ordinary arrests made under the Code of Criminal Procedure or its successor legislation.
statement_analysis.reason: D.K. Basu guidelines apply to ALL forms of arrest and detention — ordinary criminal arrests, custodial situations, and preventive detention. They are not limited to special detention laws.

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 22(2), even after a magistrate authorises custody beyond the initial 24-hour period, the arrested person's right to consult a lawyer of their choice under Article 22(1) continues throughout the period of custody.
statement_analysis.reason: The right to consult a lawyer under Article 22(1) is not extinguished after the initial production before a magistrate — it continues as a safeguard throughout the custodial period in ordinary arrest situations.

statement_analysis.statement: Post-Maneka Gandhi (1978), a preventive detention law that satisfies all the procedural requirements of Article 22(4)–(7) is automatically immune from challenge under Articles 14 and 19.
statement_analysis.reason: Maneka Gandhi's triple test requires that detention laws additionally satisfy Articles 14 (non-arbitrariness) and 19 (reasonable restriction) — compliance with Article 22's procedural requirements alone does not immunise the law from challenge under other fundamental rights.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Only three' is a strong distractor because students who correctly identify Statement 2 as false but mistakenly accept Statement 4 (assuming Article 22 compliance immunises a law) will count three correct statements.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: D.K. Basu guidelines are enforceable under Article 21 — Correct.
Statement 2: D.K. Basu applies to ALL arrests, not just preventive detention — 'exclusively' makes this incorrect.
Statement 3: Right to consult lawyer under Article 22(1) continues throughout custody, not just at the point of arrest — Correct.
Statement 4: Post-Maneka, Article 22 compliance does NOT immunise from Articles 14 and 19 challenge — 'automatically immune' is a false scope extension. Incorrect.
Statements 1 and 3 correct → 'Only two' → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 4 exploits the pre-Maneka understanding from Gopalan — that Article 22 compliance was sufficient to sustain a detention law. Post-Maneka, this is no longer true. Students who have partial knowledge of the Gopalan-to-Maneka evolution may accept Statement 4 as reflecting the current law, without recognising that Maneka specifically overruled this immunity.
solution.final_explanation:
This question integrates three concepts: D.K. Basu's expansion of Article 21, the scope of Article 22(1)'s lawyer-consultation right, and Maneka Gandhi's dismantling of Article 22 as a self-contained code.

| Statement | Verdict |
|---|---|
| S1: D.K. Basu guidelines enforceable under Article 21 | Correct |
| S2: D.K. Basu applies ONLY to preventive detention | Incorrect — applies to all arrests |
| S3: Article 22(1) lawyer right continues throughout custody | Correct |
| S4: Article 22 compliance immunises law from Articles 14 and 19 | Incorrect — Maneka Gandhi overruled this |

Only two statements are correct → option (b).

Value Addition:
• D.K. Basu requirements include: police identification cards, memo of arrest, informing relatives/friends, medical examination of the arrested person.
• These requirements are now also reflected in legislative provisions of BNSS 2023 (successor to CrPC).
• Non-compliance with D.K. Basu guidelines constitutes contempt of court — a more powerful enforcement mechanism than mere statutory violation.

solution.concept_anchor: ADM Jabalpur overruled by Puttaswamy — Articles 20 and 21 always enforceable
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because both A and R are correct, leading students who identify both as true to choose (b) without checking whether R causally explains A.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. ADM Jabalpur (1976) held that Article 21 was the sole repository of the right against arbitrary detention, and its suspension during Emergency meant no habeas corpus challenge — overruled by Puttaswamy (2017).

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. The 44th Amendment (1978) amended Article 359 to explicitly exclude Articles 20 and 21 from the President's power to suspend enforcement of fundamental rights — they are always enforceable.

Step 3: Does R explain A? — Yes. The reason Puttaswamy was able to overrule ADM Jabalpur is precisely because the constitutional framework after the 44th Amendment — which excluded Articles 20 and 21 from suspension — made ADM Jabalpur's rationale untenable. R directly explains why ADM Jabalpur's position could not survive the post-44th Amendment constitutional framework.
Both A and R correct, R explains A → select option (a).
solution.final_explanation:
ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla (1976) was decided when the Constitution permitted the President to suspend enforcement of virtually all fundamental rights under Article 359. The Supreme Court controversially held that Article 21 provided the only protection against arbitrary detention, and once its enforcement was suspended, no habeas corpus petition could challenge detention — even if the detention was arbitrary.

• Assertion (A) — Correct: Puttaswamy (2017) overruled ADM Jabalpur — holding that Articles 20 and 21 are always enforceable and cannot be suspended under Article 359.
• Reason (R) — Correct: The 44th Amendment (1978) explicitly amended Article 359 to exclude Articles 20 and 21 from the President's suspension power. This was a direct legislative response to ADM Jabalpur's dangerous precedent.
• Causal connection — Present: R explains A. The constitutional basis for ADM Jabalpur was removed by the 44th Amendment — which is precisely why Puttaswamy could overrule it. The amendment created the constitutional foundation that made ADM Jabalpur's reasoning obsolete.

Both A and R correct, R explains A → option (a).

Value Addition:
• Justice H.R. Khanna's lone dissent in ADM Jabalpur is considered one of the most courageous judicial acts in Indian legal history.
• The 44th Amendment was enacted specifically to constitutionally foreclose a repetition of Emergency-era judicial overreach.
• Puttaswamy (2017) also recognised the right to privacy — making it one of the most consequential Supreme Court judgments of the 21st century.

solution.concept_anchor: Detention void vs voidable — procedural non-compliance consequence
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) 'voidable at the discretion of the detaining authority' is deceptive because it sounds like a measured corrective response — giving the government a chance to rectify — when in fact constitutional violations render detention void ab initio.
elimination_logic: Identify the blank: The question asks for the legal consequence of failure to comply with Article 22 safeguards.
Eliminate (a): 'Irregularity that courts may overlook' fundamentally mischaracterises the constitutional importance of Article 22 safeguards — they are substantive rights, not procedural niceties.

Eliminate (b): 'Voidable at the discretion of the detaining authority' inverts the correct position — the authority does not get to decide whether its own violation matters; courts declare the detention void.
Eliminate (d): 'Suspended' is not a legal category for detention orders — detention is either valid or void.
Confirm (c): Non-compliance with Article 22 safeguards renders detention VOID — not merely irregular or voidable. Courts order immediate release under habeas corpus.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) fabricates a 'voidable at the authority's discretion' standard — this sounds administratively reasonable (the government gets to fix its own error) but is constitutionally incorrect. Courts have consistently held that Article 22 violations do not create a window for the authority to cure the defect — the detention is void from the moment of violation, and the detenu is entitled to immediate release.
solution.final_explanation:
The consequence of non-compliance with Article 22's procedural safeguards is one of the most exam-critical distinctions in preventive detention law.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Procedural failures under Article 22 are not administrative irregularities that courts may overlook. They are constitutional violations with the gravest consequence — rendering the detention void.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The concept of 'voidable at the discretion of the detaining authority' does not exist in this context. The detained person's constitutional rights cannot be subject to the government's willingness to acknowledge its own violation.
• Option (c) — Correct: Non-compliance with Article 22 safeguards — whether failure to communicate grounds, failure to refer to the Advisory Board within time, failure to consider a representation, or communicating grounds in an unknown language — renders the detention order VOID. Courts issue habeas corpus ordering immediate release.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: 'Suspended' is not a recognised legal status for detention orders — the order either stands or falls.

Value Addition:
• The void vs voidable distinction: a void order has no legal effect from its inception; a voidable order requires a court order to set it aside. Article 22 violations produce void, not voidable, orders.
• This is why courts do not 'stay' a detention order pending correction — they void it and order release.
• Even technical violations (like grounds in the wrong language) are treated with the same severity as substantive violations.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 22 not self-contained code — Article 19 challenge post-Maneka

statement_analysis.statement: A State Legislature can enact a preventive detention law under Entry 3 of the Concurrent List that permits detention purely for the exercise of the right to free speech, provided the law also complies with all Article 22 procedural safeguards.
statement_analysis.reason: Post-Maneka Gandhi, a preventive detention law cannot impose unreasonable restrictions on Article 19(1)(a) (free speech) — Article 22 procedural compliance does not immunise a law that effectively punishes the exercise of a fundamental freedom. Such a law would fail the Article 19(2) reasonable restriction test.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 22 operates as a self-contained code for preventive detention, and a law that complies with its provisions cannot be challenged under Article 19 on the ground that it imposes unreasonable restrictions on fundamental freedoms.
statement_analysis.reason: This was the pre-Maneka Gandhi (Gopalan) position. Post-Maneka, Article 22 is NOT a self-contained code — preventive detention laws must additionally satisfy Article 19's reasonable restriction test, and Article 22 compliance alone does not bar an Article 19 challenge.

statement_analysis.statement: A preventive detention law enacted by Parliament under Entry 9 of the Union List for reasons connected with the security of India must comply with the minimum procedural safeguards in Article 22 — it cannot derive immunity from these safeguards by virtue of its subject-matter under the Union List.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 22's minimum procedural safeguards are constitutional requirements that apply regardless of the legislative entry under which the law is enacted — no subject-matter entry in the Seventh Schedule grants immunity from Article 22's procedural floor.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) '1 only' is deceptive because Statement 1 is clearly incorrect — students who identify Statement 1 as wrong may assume Statement 2 is a correct statement of current law (Gopalan's silo theory) without recognising it was overruled.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: A law detaining persons for exercising free speech fails the Article 19(1)(a)/19(2) test — Article 22 compliance cannot save it post-Maneka. Incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: 'Article 22 is a self-contained code' is the overruled Gopalan position — post-Maneka, Article 19 challenge is fully available. Incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: Article 22's minimum safeguards apply to all preventive detention laws regardless of legislative entry — Correct. Not the incorrect statement.
Statements 1 and 2 are NOT correct → select option (d): 1 and 2.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the most dangerous trap — it states the pre-Maneka (Gopalan) legal position as if it were current law. Students who have surface knowledge of 'Gopalan said Article 22 is self-contained' but haven't internalised that Maneka overruled this will accept Statement 2 as a correct statement of law. The question asks which statements are NOT correct — making Statement 2's acceptance the error that leads to a wrong answer.
solution.final_explanation:
The relationship between Article 22 and Article 19 is one of the most doctrinally significant areas in preventive detention law.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: A law that effectively detains persons for exercising their right to free speech would violate Article 19(1)(a) read with Article 19(2) — no law authorising such detention could pass the reasonable restriction test, regardless of Article 22 procedural compliance.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The 'self-contained code' characterisation is the Gopalan (1950) position, definitively overruled by Maneka Gandhi (1978). Post-Maneka, Article 22 does not operate in isolation — preventive detention laws must satisfy Articles 14, 19, and 21 as well.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The legislative entry under which a preventive detention law is enacted (Entry 9 Union List, Entry 3 Concurrent List) determines Parliament's/State's competence to enact it — but does not exempt the law from Article 22's constitutional procedural floor.

Value Addition:
• The post-Maneka framework applies the 'triple test' to all laws affecting fundamental rights, not just detention laws.
• COFEPOSA survived Article 19(1)(g) challenge because the economic security rationale satisfied the Article 19(6) reasonable restriction test.
• The legislative entry determines WHO can make the law — the fundamental rights provisions determine WHETHER the law is constitutionally valid.

solution.final_explanation:
A clause-by-clause map of Article 22 is a foundational requirement for this topic.

Correct matching: A–3, B–1, C–4, D–2.

• A (Article 22(1)): Right to be informed of grounds of arrest AND right to consult a lawyer of one's choice — the two-in-one right for ordinary arrest.
• B (Article 22(3)): The exclusion clause — enemy aliens and persons detained under preventive detention laws are excluded from Article 22(1) and (2) protections.
• C (Article 22(4)): Sets the 3-month ceiling — no detention beyond 3 months without an Advisory Board reporting sufficient cause.
• D (Advisory Board composition): Members must be persons who are, or have been, or are qualified to be appointed as High Court judges — ensuring quasi-judicial quality.

Value Addition:
• Article 22(2) contains the 24-hour magistrate production rule — distinct from Article 22(1)'s lawyer/grounds rights.
• Article 22(5) contains the right to make a representation AND the 'as soon as may be' obligation to communicate grounds.
• Article 22(6) is the non-disclosure clause — authority MAY withhold facts against public interest.
• Article 22(7) is the Parliamentary override for extended detention without Advisory Board.

solution.concept_anchor: Habeas corpus — void detention — successive order limits

statement_analysis.statement: In a successful habeas corpus petition challenging a preventive detention order, a court may order the immediate release of the detenu — but this does not prevent the detaining authority from issuing a fresh detention order based on genuinely independent new grounds.
statement_analysis.reason: Habeas corpus grants release from the specific invalid order — it does not permanently bar re-detention if the authority has fresh, independent grounds. The Haradhan Saha principle confirms that successive detention on new grounds is constitutionally permissible.

statement_analysis.statement: A preventive detenu who is released pursuant to a habeas corpus order may apply for bail before the Sessions Court to prevent any further detention while the government considers a fresh detention order.
statement_analysis.reason: Bail is not the mechanism available in preventive detention — the detenu is released by the habeas corpus order itself. There is no 'anticipatory' bail mechanism in preventive detention law equivalent to criminal procedure; the government may issue a fresh order at any point on new grounds.

statement_analysis.statement: A court conducting a habeas corpus review of a preventive detention order evaluates the procedural compliance of the detention and the relevance of the grounds — but does not assess whether the detaining authority's subjective conclusion about the necessity of detention was correct.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the established judicial review standard — courts in habeas corpus examine procedure and ground-relevance but do not substitute their assessment of whether detention was actually necessary. Subjective satisfaction is reserved for the detaining authority.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) '1, 2 and 3' is a strong distractor because all three statements appear superficially related to judicial remedies in preventive detention, and students who do not carefully parse Statement 2 will mark all three as correct.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Release by habeas corpus does not bar fresh detention on new grounds — correct position under Haradhan Saha. Correct.

Statement 2: There is no bail mechanism in preventive detention to prevent a fresh order — release flows from the habeas corpus order itself; the government can issue a new order at any time on fresh grounds. Incorrect.
Statement 3: Habeas corpus review is limited to procedural compliance and ground-relevance — courts do not assess the merits of the subjective satisfaction. Correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct → select option (c): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 fabricates a mechanism — 'anticipatory bail against preventive detention' — that does not exist in Indian law. The concept of bail in criminal procedure is well-known, and students may assume an analogous mechanism exists in preventive detention. It does not. Release in preventive detention comes only through the habeas corpus order or government revocation — there is no bail bridge between one detention order and the next.
solution.final_explanation:
The interface between habeas corpus, subjective satisfaction, and successive detention is a multi-concept area requiring precise understanding.

• Statement 1 — Correct: A habeas corpus order grants release from the specific void detention — it is not a permanent immunity. If the government has genuinely fresh grounds, it can issue a new detention order. Courts will scrutinise whether the new grounds are independent or recycled.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: There is no bail mechanism between a successful habeas corpus order and a potential fresh detention order. The detenu is free following the habeas corpus order — but if the government issues a new valid detention order, the only recourse is another habeas corpus petition.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Courts in habeas corpus review examine procedure and relevance of grounds — this is objective review. They do not second-guess the detaining authority's subjective conclusion that detention was necessary — this respects the constitutional design vesting this assessment in the executive.

Value Addition:
• This three-part structure (habeas corpus scope + no bail + subjective satisfaction limits) is frequently combined into single UPSC questions.
• The 'anticipatory bail' concept exists in ordinary criminal law under Section 438 CrPC (now BNSS) — it has no analogue in preventive detention.
• Mala fides and non-application of mind, if proved, are additional grounds for habeas corpus beyond procedural violations.
